doc.title: Carter Benny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Playing the clarinet as a doubling instrument
summary: He picked up clarinet as a dance-band double, probably with Charlie Johnson, and let it taper off in the mid-forties.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: All right. Can we move to another instrument?
Please do.
The clarinet.
Oh, my. Please don’t. [laughter]
Well, many critics, in fact, all critics that have chosen to deal with the subject, have lamented that you gave up the clarinet relatively early. When did you . . .
Well, would you weigh that against the number of people who didn’t lament it?
[laughter]
Well, let’s put it this way. No one who mentioned it said that they wish you had given it up sooner.
[laughs] That was really the point I was trying to make.
Well, before it gets too convoluted . . .
Yeah, that’s right.
. . . and before we have you giving it up, how did you begin playing it?

I don’t know, just . . . you know, at that time when you played with the orchestra, a dance orchestra, you usually had to play the clarinet, you know, as a double, and so I picked it up. And some time later I put it down.
Would the picking up of the instrument happen, just logically, around the time you began to work in some of these orchestras?
Yes, maybe. Maybe when I . . . yeah, went with Billy Fowler or maybe even Charlie Johnson, I might have. I don’t know.
Because by 1928 you were already recording on it occasionally.
The clarinet, really?
Yeah.
Well, then I must have started it when I went with Charlie Johnson.
And you continued to play it, I guess, into the forties, maybe late . . .
Yes, I guess so.
’45, ’46. Was there a conscious decision at some point to give it up, or did it just kind of . . .
Just kind of tapered off, I suppose, you know.
